question.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-2$ |

$$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}.$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{f(1)+1}{g(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+x)^{′}}{(g(x)-x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1} & ={\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)+1}{{g}^{′}(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{′}(x)+1)^{′}}{({g}^{′}(x)-1)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)},\end{aligned}
$$

and this time, when we substitute $x=1,$ we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{{g}^{″}(1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{-2} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}=-2.$
